extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, equity masters/commissioners, and judges handling patent accounting and remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and practice for computing and litigating an infringer's profits in patent cases: selecting and proving the proper standard of comparison, what counts as the 'advantage', masters' powers and duties in taking accounts, procedure for draft/final reports, and how exceptions are to be presented and reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of the standard of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The complainant normally selects what appears to him to be the proper standard of comparison and must produce evidence to show the advantage the defendant derived from using the complainant's invention over what he could have derived from using that selected standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary for the complainant to prove that the selected standard was absolutely the next best available (impossible to prove). If the defendant is dissatisfied he may select another and produce evidence of its utility and cheapness; the master will decide which selection is proper and that standard will be used in the accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the 'true' standard of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The true standard of comparison is the prior process or thing which, next to the complainant's invention, could have been most advantageously used by the defendant in place of that invention at the time he used it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination should consider both comparative utility and comparative cost (the advantage is the equalized result of both elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard need not have been actually used by defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's proffered standard of comparison need not have been used by him at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of the utility of such a standard (vs. the invention) may be drawn from persons who used both under the same conditions or from any source capable of furnishing convincing proof; even if used, defendants may show others obtained better results and claim that superiority in the accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of 'advantage' (profits) — gains and savings
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantage derived from the use of the invention may consist of affirmative gains and savings from loss (e.g., savings in materials, labor, fuel, or increased value of byproducts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: savings of lime and sulphuric acid; increased value of glycerine; savings of coal and labor compared to the cheapest prior process. Both gains and cost-savings are relevant to measuring profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of substitutes and improvements in defendant's device
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant's machine differs from the patented invention only by substitution of equivalents, it is treated as if it were the complainant's unchanged invention; but if the defendant's machine contains an improvement upon the complainant's invention, the defendant is entitled to credit for the improvement's contribution to profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule applies to machines and to processes or other patent subjects; credit the infringer for any non-infringing improvements that contributed to profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability of Section 725 to mere making/selling
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for computing advantage (Section 725) does not apply to cases consisting only of making and selling a patented article, except where the patented article is used as a component of a much larger article made and sold by the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to use alternative products as standards of comparison in pure make-and-sell cases is generally without foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on infringer's profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest on profits is allowed from the date of the master's report that ascertains those profits or from the date of their first judicial ascertainment; allowance of interest is discretionary with the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If profits are first ascertained by the court rather than the master, interest may run from that judicial ascertainment date; courts exercise discretion in awarding interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant's burden to introduce evidence at accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: After an interlocutory decree directing an accounting, it is the complainant's duty to introduce evidence before the master to prove the amount of the defendant's profits; the master will pass upon whatever evidence the complainant produces, in light of the defendant's evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The master is not required to suggest lines of proof or accounting theory; each party must initially pay their own costs and may be taxed later depending on the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of accounts and defendants' sworn statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity practice requires parties accounting before a master to bring in accounts in debtor-and-creditor form; masters commonly summon defendants to bring in sworn statements of infringing devices and other data enabling the plaintiff to establish his case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the practice's propriety has been questioned, courts have held such statements can and should specify debit and credit items. The summons should be limited to matters appropriate to an account in debtor-and-creditor form (manufacture, sales, amounts received, and items of credit like cost of materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of evidence the master may consider
rubrics_metrics.description: The master may base his report on any evidence taken in the case prior to the interlocutory decree, documents and depositions introduced for the accounting, viva voce testimony taken before him (anywhere in the world), and his personal examination of structures or processes involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If required documents are not produced voluntarily, the master may compel production and may certify for commissions to take depositions under court procedures or statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording of viva voce testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When testimony is taken viva voce before a master, either party may require that it be taken down in writing so it can be used by the court if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the record for use with the master's report and in later court review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of defendant's books and papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The master must give due consideration to the defendant's rights that his books and papers be scrutinized only insofar as they are material to the issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of inspection should be limited to materials relevant to contested items; the master has authority to direct proceedings to fairly ascertain the accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's authority to order accounts and enforce obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: The master has full authority to direct necessary acts and proceedings for justice of the case, including ordering the defendant to furnish accounts or calculations by a certain day; noncompliance may constitute contempt of court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders served by any disinterested person must be obeyed or the defendant risks contempt—used to compel production of accounts derived from defendant's books when necessary for decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and preservation of objections to evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to evidence must be made when the objectionable evidence is offered, question put, or answer given; if the master is present he should rule at once and an immediate appeal must be taken if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the master rules against the objector and the objector wishes to appeal, he must move immediately to the court to direct the master to reverse; failure to timely object or move may foreclose review except by immediate motion or exceptions to the master's report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when master absent at deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If the master is not present when a deposition is taken, the notary or magistrate should note objections on the deposition and take down the evidence; the objections can later be brought before the master and reviewed on exceptions to the master's report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notaries lack authority to rule; objections preserved on deposition permit the master/court to consider admissibility later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master's duty to determine extent of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The master must determine the extent (and in some circumstances the existence) of the defendant's infringement to enable ascertainment of profits; where the interlocutory decree specifies the doings, the issue may be purely quantitative, but where it does not, the master may decide infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though some courts permit masters to decide infringement issues, the most convenient practice is for the court to decide infringement before entering an interlocutory decree; in some jurisdictions supplemental bills are required to add infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation of profits by kinds of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alleged infringements are of several sorts, the master generally ought to report profits as separate items for each kind so courts can render decree for part or all according to infringement rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rule of convenience and may be departed from when separating profits would be difficult or unnecessary (e.g., where two kinds of machines were used together and profits cannot be separated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft report procedure and opportunity to correct
rubrics_metrics.description: The master should prepare a draft report after testimony and argument so parties can correct any misapprehensions; parties dissatisfied must file exceptions to the draft report pointing to each alleged error, after which the master may reconsider and file a final report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No new evidence may be introduced after the draft report (exceptions proceedings are for errors apparent on the record). Failing to file exceptions before the master risks later courts disregarding those exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and advisory nature of the final report
rubrics_metrics.description: The final report is advisory to the court and must be confined to points the interlocutory decree directed the master to ascertain; it should contain final conclusions of fact (reviewable only on exceptions) and conclusions of law which the court may verify or correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final report should not include criticism of the decree or suggestions of judicial action; courts may correct legal conclusions before entering final decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for precise exceptions to master's reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to a master's report must be aimed with precision at the alleged errors and supported with references to the particular evidence or master's statements relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant or complainant affirmative exceptions must cite particular evidence; negative exceptions challenging admissibility should specify evidence objected to when possible, or require the master to make a special statement in his final report of the evidence that convinced him if the exceptor claims there was none.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and handling of defendants' exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant's exceptions fall into four classes: (1) evidence shows no profit/no damage; (2) evidence shows master's finding too large; (3) no admissible evidence proving profit/damage; (4) no admissible evidence proving profit/damage to the extent found. Affirmative exceptions must specify evidence; negative exceptions should identify particular objections or require special statements from the master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative exceptions require specification of the evidence relied on; negative exceptions that deny the presence of evidence should ask the master to state what evidence convinced him for inclusion in the final report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant's exceptions — classes and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant's exceptions may (1) assert evidence shows larger profits/damages than reported, or (2) assert the master erred in admitting inadmissible evidence; both are affirmative and must be supported by references to particular evidence or by special statements of the master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When made to a draft report, complainant's exceptions must reference particular evidence; when made to a final report, they must either refer to particular evidence or to master statements that obviate that necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall outline of master's role and finality of findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The master's function is to investigate only the questions referred by the court, take testimony, receive evidence, and decide conclusions of fact which will stand unless clearly erroneous; draft report should state those conclusions alone unless the court/parties direct otherwise, and final report should include final conclusions and only such evidence statements as parties lawfully require to be attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no direction to report evidence is given, a master's report containing only his findings is conclusive unless successfully excepted to; the system emphasizes limiting review to errors specifically pointed out and preserving efficiency of referral.
